case_name: Mahavir Prashad Gupta and Another v State of National Capital Territory of Delhi and Others
respondent: State of National Capital Territory of Delhi
facts: On November 6, 1997, 2nd respondent filed a complaint with the Station House Officer, Police Station, Vasant Vihar, New Delhi.

In the complaint, it was stated that 2nd respondent had handed over a consignment of 400 Video Cassette Recorders and 8 sets of 20" Colour Televisions with remote and woofers packed in 417 packages to M/s. Road Transport Corporation (hereinafter called "the said firm") for transporting to Guwahati in Assam.
It was also stated that the said firm had sent Vehicle No. DBL-4365 to the complainant's godown and loaded the consignment in the vehicle.
It was stated that the consignment had not been delivered.
It was stated that the complainant had learnt that the consignment was never sent to Guwahati and was kept by the said firm.
In the complaint, it was claimed that there was breach of trust and forgery on the part of petitioners who were the proprietors of the said firm.
On the basis of this complaint, the police called the petitioners at the Vasant Vihar Police Station on November 8, 1997.
The petitioner appeared before the police and brought the attention of the police to a letter, dated October 27, 1997, sent by the petitioners.
Thereafter, the police registered an F.I.R. on November 9, 1997.
On December 16, 1997, the petitioners filed this Criminal Writ Petition No. 905 of 1997 in the High Court of Delhi.
In this petition, it was prayed that the F.I.R. registered by the police be quashed.

It was claimed that 2nd respondent and the police are acting in abuse and excess of authority conferred by law and are subjecting the petitioners to harassment of criminal proceedings without there being any sufficient ground for taking action against the petitioners.
issues: The power of quashing criminal proceedings must be exercised very sparingly and with circumspection.
The Court would not be justified in embarking upon an enquiry as to the reliability or genuineness or otherwise of the allegations made in the F.I.R. or the complaint.
The extraordinary or inherent powers did not confer an arbitrary jurisdiction on the Court to act according to its whim or caprice.
petitioner_arguments: There was no case of breach of trust and/or of forgery.
The complaint was a false complaint made merely with the intention of misusing process of law and subjecting the petitioners to undue harassment.
On these facts, the police should have refused to register an F.I.R. and should have directed the parties to settle their disputes and differences in a civil court.
court_reasoning: The complaint did not disclose any offence.
It would have been dereliction of duty on the part of police to look at facts outside the complaint.
The F.I.R. itself, on the fact of it, did not make out any offence.
holding: The petition was ultimately dismissed by the High Court of Delhi.
